source.title: Multilingual Sequence-to-Sequence Models for Hebrew NLP
source.authors: Matan Eyal; Hila Noga; Roee Aharoni; I. Szpektor; Reut Tsarfaty

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares downstream task scores across mT5 sizes, bearing on downstream performance with scale, but does not measure pretraining loss or reproduce the original scaling-law measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling-law work and reports mT5 sizes from 300M to 13B, but its results are fine-tuned Hebrew downstream task metrics, not held-out pretraining losses, compute sweeps, or fitted scaling laws. The mT5 size comparisons in Tables 1 and 2 are included; referenced baseline scores are not treated as mT5 scaling results. The lemmatization table's flattened values do not establish which mT5 size achieved 95.53, so that value is not assigned to a size.
record.test_reason: Fine-tunes all five public mT5 sizes (300M–13B) on Hebrew downstream tasks and reports scores per size. That bears weakly on V6 (downstream performance rising with scale) in a new setting: Hebrew, a morphologically rich language, using text-to-text fine-tuning. It fits no relationship and does not measure pretraining loss, so 'predictably' is not tested. T3 fits better than T2 because the paper's aim is a Hebrew benchmark comparison, not a scaling question.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that fine-tuned mT5 in a text-to-text formulation beats prior encoder-only Hebrew baselines on all evaluated tasks. They recommend multilingual seq2seq models for Hebrew and other morphologically rich languages. They say larger mT5 models perform better but cost more hardware and time. They do not isolate the contributions of size, data and architecture.
record.recipe_differences: Fine-tunes multilingual mT5 sizes on Hebrew downstream benchmarks and reports task metrics; it does not measure held-out pretraining loss or compute-optimal allocation as the original scaling studies do.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream scores vary by task and metric; sentiment F1 and POS tagging mset are not strictly monotonic across adjacent mT5 sizes.
record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The paper does not pretrain new models or isolate the contributions of model size, multilingual pretraining data, and architecture. No uncertainty estimates are supplied for the tabulated downstream scores. The paper notes that larger mT5 models require more powerful hardware and longer training and inference.
record.rows_left_out: The Table 2 lemmatization values are flattened and do not identify which mT5 size corresponds to 95.53; that result is omitted rather than assigned to a model. Referenced baseline scores are not results for the mT5 size sweep.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss is measured and no models are pretrained.
No shape variation at fixed parameter count.
No power-law fit for fine-tuning or transfer.
Predictability: no functional fit to size, no prediction from pretraining loss, only five sizes, and no uncertainty on Table 1/2 scores.

missing.what: Item-level size comparison on ParaShoot. Of 519 XXL exact matches, small scored F1 0 on 167. Small correctly answered 49 questions XXL missed.
Lemmatization mset for mT5. The table lists only two mT5 values (95.13, 95.53) for five sizes, so the size assignment cannot be read.

record.verdict_notes: Evidence for V6 is weak: five off-the-shelf checkpoints, a single fine-tuning recipe (4096 steps, constant learning rate 1e-3), no seeds for Table 1/2, and no fitted trend. Sizes are confounded with nothing else within mT5, but the pretraining data are fixed across sizes. Baseline-model scores (mBERT, AlephBERT and others) are cited from other papers and are correctly excluded from the rows.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fit or prediction of larger-run held-out loss.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token analysis.
No comparison of depth, width, or architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No test of power-law loss in another modality or pretraining regime; downstream fine-tuning scores are not loss-law measurements.

Tests downstream task scores across mT5 sizes in Hebrew, but does not fit a predictive relationship, test prediction from pretraining loss, or evaluate other downstream settings beyond the reported tasks.
Does not test how scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations depend on fitting choices.

relationships.condition: ParaShoot (EM, F1), NEMO token and morpheme NER, BMC NER, and UD segmentation; mT5 Small→XXL
relationships.reason: Scores rise monotonically with size. Examples: ParaShoot F1 48.71→77.5, NEMO morph F1 62.08→88.65 (r1–r25, r31–r35); appendix seeds agree (r41–r44).
relationships.display_finding: Scores increased monotonically with size, including ParaShoot F1 from 48.71 to 77.5 and NEMO morpheme F1 from 62.08 to 88.65, with agreement across additional seeds.

relationships.condition: Sentiment analysis F1 and UD POS tagging mset
relationships.reason: Sentiment barely moves with scale (87.55→89.61, with a dip at Base). POS dips from Base 95.9 to Large 95.58 before rising (r26–r30, r36–r40).
relationships.display_finding: Sentiment F1 rises only from 87.55 to 89.61 with a dip at Base, while POS performance falls from 95.9 at Base to 95.58 at Large before recovering.
